INTERAGENCY AUTISM COORDINATING COMMITTEE
2023 SUMMARY OF ADVANCES
in Autism Research  
At-a-Glance 
OVERVIEW
The Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee (IACC) is a federal advisory committee that provides 
advice to the Secretary of Health and Human Services. The IACC includes federal agency representatives 
and public members representing the autism community. The IACC selected their top 20 most significant 
autism research advances published in 2023. The articles are divided into categories that correspond  
to categories in the IACC Strategic Plan. This at-a-glance version of the Summary of Advances provides  
a one-sentence summary of the findings of each research study that is described in more detail in the  
full-length publication. The full publication is available here: https://iacc.hhs.gov/publications/ 
summary-of-advances/2023/.
SCREENING AND DIAGNOSIS
• Differences in how Black and White children respond to the Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ) 
can lead to unequal accuracy of results that may reinforce racial inequalities. [LINK]
• Data from electronic health records can be used to help detect autism in children by 1 year of age,  
complementing other screening methods. [LINK] 
•  Eye-tracking technology, which tracks where children look during social interactions, can reliably identify 
autism in children between 16 and 30 months old. [LINK]
• A tablet-based digital app that captures behavioral signs of autism can be used to improve screening 
of children from diverse populations in non-research settings, complementing other screening methods. 
[LINK] 
BIOLOGY 
• Key behavioral features of autistic people may be explained by differences in the strength of connections 
between brain regions and the activity of certain genes. [LINK]
•  Most autistic people improve in their communication skills as they reach adolescence but vary more in 
their social skills, with some improving, while others remain stable or gain and then lose skills. [LINK]
2
GENETIC AND ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS 
• Microbes in the digestive systems of autistic people differ from those of neurotypical people and can 
impact behavior and health, suggesting that gut-brain communication plays a role in autism. [LINK]
INTERVENTIONS 
• The Joint Attention Symbolic Play Engagement and Regulation (JASPER) intervention improved play skills 
in young children with autism. [LINK]
• Lower verbal ability is linked to behaviors that interfere with daily living and social participation,  
but augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) use alone is not correlated with fewer of these 
behaviors. [LINK]
• Autistic children who received individualized intervention at 18 months showed improved social and  
language skills when compared to children who started at 27 months. [LINK]
• Wearable biosensors and machine learning tested in autistic youth staying in psychiatric hospitals were 
able to predict aggressive behaviors 3 minutes before they started. [LINK]
• Targeted early intervention can promote spoken language skills among autistic preschoolers with limited 
spoken language. [LINK]
SERVICES AND SUPPORTS 
•  Earlier diagnoses, when combined with appropriate and timely interventions, could reduce disparities  
in cognitive health outcomes for Black autistic children. [LINK]
•  Family navigation can improve participation in IDEA Part C early intervention services among Hispanic 
and non-Hispanic autistic children. [LINK]
• In rural areas, Black and Hispanic children have the fewest autism resources, while American Indian,  
Alaska Native, and Hispanic children have the fewest autism resources in urban areas. [LINK]
LIFESPAN 
• Autistic individuals with and without intellectual disability experience changes in behavioral health 
during adulthood that suggest the need for access to supports throughout adulthood. [LINK]
• Analysis of students’ individualized education plans (IEPs) highlights disparities in autistic adolescents’ 
transition planning and the need for more supportive services to meet postsecondary goals. [LINK]
• Autistic females experience higher rates of self-harm, and co-occurring mental health conditions  
that are associated with increased risk of self-harm and suicide are experienced by both autistic males 
and females. [LINK]
• Compared to non-autistic adolescents, from ages 14 to 22 years old, autistic adolescents experience  
a higher and rising prevalence of co-occurring health conditions. [LINK]
INFRASTRUCTURE AND PREVALENCE 
• CDC’s Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network data from 2020 estimates  
that 1 in 36 8-year-old children in the United States are autistic. [LINK]
